1:
Jerome traces the question to the coin: the disciples, having seen one piece of money pay for Peter and for the Lord, concluded from the equality of ransom that Peter was preferred. Chrysostom notes they were ashamed to show the feeling and so asked in general rather than why Peter had been honoured above them, and that the three distinguished at the transfiguration provoked no such grief as the singling out of one. Robertson reads the particle as pointing back to the tax-gatherers, who had singled Peter out, and concludes his primacy was not yet admitted. Ellicott adds the choice of the Three to the promise made to Peter, and finds the less distinguished jealous while Zebedee's sons conceded nothing.

Lightfoot observes the ambitious dispute mostly followed the mention of Christ's death, the dream of an earthly kingdom so possessing their minds, sucked in with their first milk, that repeated mention of a shameful death did not drive it thence. Calvin says it more sharply: the prediction had made them sad, yet they fell to disputing the primacy as though they had tasted the nectar the poets feign, the flesh shaking off uneasiness so that they left what grieved them out of view and fixed on the resurrection. He names two faults: they demanded repose and wages beforehand like soldiers who had served their time, and they strove to excel each other instead of securing for their brethren as large a share as for themselves. Henry apportions the offices each expected: Peter lord-chancellor for the keys, Judas lord-treasurer for the bag, John as favourite, Andrew first called and so first preferred; they looked so much at the crown that they forgot the yoke and the cross. Barnes reports from Mark that they had disputed in the way, and from Luke that Jesus perceived the thought of their heart, which he takes to imply omniscience.

Jerome gives two readings of the child set in the midst, one whose tender age should express the innocence they wanted, and a deeper one, that Christ set himself in the midst, a little one come not to be ministered unto but to minister. Origen offers a third, that the little one is the Holy Spirit, who humbled himself when called and was set in the midst of the disciples' reason, so that men turned from all else are likened to the children God gave the Saviour. Jerome presses that the age is not enjoined but the innocence, which infants have by their years and the apostles must reach by striving: a child is not obstinate in anger, bears no injury in mind, is unmoved at the sight of a fair woman, and does not think one thing while saying another. Hilary extends the name to all who believe through the hearing of faith, following their father, bearing no hate and trusting what they are told.

What the turning means is pressed hardest by the moderns. Clarke takes it as deliverance from the national prejudice that looked for a temporal kingdom, and quotes Saady, that infant hearts, free from avarice, care no more for a handful of silver than for a handful of dust. Ellicott warns against reading a later technical sense into the word and puts the weight on the warning: men disputing precedence showed they were not in the kingdom, so even the chief of the apostles was self-excluded when he gloried in his primacy; and to humble oneself in order to be great would reduce humility to hypocrisy. Robertson notes the double negative shuts them out of the kingdom altogether, let alone its big places. Calvin supplies the definition: the humble man claims no merit before God, does not despise his brethren or aim to be thought above them, but reckons it enough to be one of the members, desiring only that the Head be exalted.
5:
Who the little one is must be settled first. Gill reads it metaphorically, one who is as this child for modesty and humility, free from pride and ambition and envy, the receiving being of Christ's disciples into men's houses or hearts. Clarke agrees the term means a disciple only, the child having served above as the emblem of one, Christ reckoning any kindness shown such a man for his sake as done to himself. Origen begins simply: a man who mortifies the lusts of manhood until he has a child's condition is converted, and the further he advances the greater he is. Calvin takes the saying for consolation, lest humility seem troublesome, since by it Christ receives us under his protection and recommends us to the favour of men, the more a man abases himself the more highly to be honoured. Henry makes the kindness Christ's own, since whoever entertains a meek Christian will not let him lose by his modesty, the less the man is in himself the more the good will is to Christ; and on the threat he notes that hell is worse than the depth of the sea, Jonah having found comfort in the deep where none ever had a grain of it in hell.

Origen raises the difficulty himself and answers twice. If one become as a little child cannot be made to stumble, how is the little one here liable? First, not all converted with a view to the likeness have reached it, each wanting as much as he falls short of a child's disposition. Then, against his own answer, he allows the perfect man may be the one called little, on the strength of the word that he who is least among you all is great, and of Paul calling himself less than the least of saints: the little one is he who humbles himself among all that believe, though an apostle or a bishop, and it is his angel that beholds the face of God.

On the offence itself the readings converge. Gill takes a man offended when he is not received, his person despised and ministry rejected, until he drops his profession. Barnes defines it as causing to fall or to sin, or putting anything in the way to hinder another's piety, and concludes it were better for such a man to die before committing the sin. Clarke bids those who act the part of the devil in tempting others hear the declaration and tremble. Calvin observes that a man who thinks too highly of himself must treat his brethren with disdain, and that the word forbids more than contempt alone, since he who gives himself no concern about the weak already withholds their due honour; the remedy being to stretch a hand to those the world despises. Ellicott hears the thought rising unbidden in a Christ-like mind, which gazes on the innocent beauty of childhood and dreads to see it marred by evil.

The millstone is identified and documented. Barnes and Robertson both make it the larger stone turned by a beast, not the handmill, Robertson adding that the adjective meaning turned by an ass had no example outside the New Testament until the papyri supplied several, and glossing the deep as the sea of the sea. Clarke cites the Scholiast on the Equites of Aristophanes and Suidas for the Greek practice of hanging a vast stone about the neck. Lightfoot distinguishes it from the small mills used to grind spices for the wound of circumcision, and takes the death for one perhaps never used among the Jews, named either to aggravate the thing or in allusion to the Dead Sea, where drowning implied devoting to execration. Ellicott agrees the Jewish law did not recognise it, reports it from the Greeks and from Augustus in cases of special infamy, and cites Jerome for its practice in Galilee.
7:
That offences must come raises the question of freedom. Chrysostom denies that the saying subverts free will, since the prophecy does not bring the offences in: it is not done because he foretold it, but he foretold it because it was certainly to come. Ellicott finds the clause and the woe uniting two truths in strange contrast: crimes recur with something like the regularity of a law, yet in each instance the offender's will was free and he is rightly held responsible. The Gloss offers the other account, that they must come because they are useful, that they which are approved may be made manifest. Barnes grounds the necessity in depravity, some always attempting to make others sin and rejoicing at success. Calvin makes it God's own purpose, who leaves his people exposed to exercise their faith and to separate believers, as the refuse and chaff, from the pure wheat. Henry turns the woe into a judicial principle: he who opened the pit and kindled the fire was accountable for all the damage that ensued, so God's making the sins of sinners serve his purposes will not secure them from his wrath.

What kind of utterance the woe is divides them. Clarke reports that some eminent critics take the word always to express sympathy in our Lord's mouth, and adds that giver and taker of the offence are both exposed to ruin. Calvin sets out two constructions, a curse on the authors of offences, the world then meaning all unbelievers, or a lament over the evils he saw coming; he prefers the second and holds no plague more destructive. Chrysostom faces the objection that one who ought to stretch out a hand instead laments, and answers that nothing was left undone, so the lament falls on men nothing the better for that care; the mourning is itself a kind of healing, since many whom advice did not profit amended when mourned for.

The hand and the eye are read of persons, not of limbs. Raban fixes the word, scandal being Greek for a stumbling-block or fall, and a man scandalizing his brother who by word or deed amiss gives him occasion of falling. Chrysostom says it is not of the body's limbs but of friends whom we esteem as limbs necessary to us, nothing being so hurtful as evil communications. Jerome works it out: if a man be united to thee as close as thy hand or eye, useful, anxious and quick to discern, and yet draw thee by the unmeetness of his behaviour toward hell, it is better to lack his kindred, and better to lead a solitary life than to lose eternal life for what this life needs. Origen applies it to office in the congregations: when one who for his practical gifts bears the name of hand becomes a hand causing others to stumble, the eye is to say it has no need of him.

The moderns keep the figure but press the sanction. Barnes holds that attachments and employments not pursuable without sin must be abandoned however dear, denies the risen body will be maimed, and takes the eternal fire for conclusive proof that the sufferings of the wicked have no end. Robertson calls the two verses one of Matthew's doublets, notes the first use in the Gospel of the word meaning ageless, and argues that making it an age-long fire must make the life age-long too, so that if the punishment is limited the life is shortened; the word for one-eyed he calls an Ionic compound the Atticists condemned and the vernacular revived. Calvin reaches the same severity otherwise: a man who hesitates to lose a limb spares it at the risk of eternal perdition. Wesley puts the reader's question and answers it: is this not a hard saying? Yes, if you take counsel with flesh and blood.
10:
Jerome reads the warning as tempering what went before: despise them not, and next your own salvation seek to heal them, though if they hold to their sins it is better you be saved than perish in company. Souls, he exclaims, have high dignity, each having an angel set over it from birth. Chrysostom pairs the two commands: above he bade them cut off the friendships of those who gave offence, here teaches honour to the saints, the perfect reckoned little ones because they seem poor and despicable. Ellicott keeps the scene in view, the child still there and perhaps folded in the arms of Jesus, and thinks some disciples' faces betrayed the half-contemptuous wonder which drew the rebuke.

What the angels of the little ones are is disputed six ways. Clarke holds the Lord here establishes the notion received by almost all nations, that every person has a guardian angel with access to God for orders. Ellicott agrees the words distinctly recognise the belief, those set over the little ones being among the noblest, angels of the Presence. Barnes denies the inference: Christ does not mean every good man to have his own guardian, as many of the Jews believed, but that the angels are in general the guards of his followers; the face he reads from earthly courts, where free access marked favour. Robertson leaves both doors open, whether a special angel stands in that intimacy or the angels merely take an interest in God's people. Henry takes a middle way, asking why we should suppose every saint has a guardian angel when every saint, as occasion requires, has a guard of them; and reads the beholding of the face as prime ministers seeing the king's, as if the strongest angels had charge of the weakest saints. Augustine settles only the last phrase: the face of God means the manifestation of himself, not any feature of a body. Cyril of Jerusalem qualifies the degree: the angels behold God not as he is but as far as they are capable, Archangels more and Thrones and Dominions more still, yet all less than his worthiness, since with the Son only the Holy Spirit rightly beholds him.

Two fathers press further into the ministry. Gregory reports from Dionysius that the lesser ranks are sent on this errand, the higher having no outward ministry, resolving it thus: they come forth by a spiritual presence while keeping themselves by contemplation where they came from, not losing the divine vision's joy. Hilary makes the angels carry up daily the prayers of those to be saved, so it is perilous to despise a man whose requests reach God by such a ministry. On the following verse the verdicts are opposite: Ellicott reports the words wanting in many of the best manuscripts, while Clarke counts five manuscripts, two versions and three fathers against them yet holds them authentic beyond doubt, the same sentence standing in the parallel place where no various reading has been found.

The parable is read at two levels. Hilary takes the one sheep for one man and under him the whole human race, Christ the seeker, the ninety and nine the heavenly host he left. Gregory counts a hundred perfect, the Creator owning that number when he had made the substance of angels and men, and explains the greater joy thus: the righteous are often slothful through security while men with wicked deeds to remember glow with more heat in their love, as a general best loves the soldier who turns from flight and presses the foe. Bede grounds it differently: there is greater matter for thanksgiving in man's restoration than in the angels' creation, since wonderfully are the angels made but more wonderfully man restored. Raban works the arithmetic: nine wants one to make ten, and lost man was sought on earth so the number might be perfect in heaven.
15:
Chrysostom notes that the Lord, having terrified those who give offence, now checks the opposite fault in those who take it, the grieved man being drawn to his grievers because the wrongdoer will not readily come for shame. He marks the words: not Accuse him nor Demand redress but Tell him his fault, since a man held down by anger or shame is stupefied as in deep slumber, and the one in his right senses must go to the one in the disease. Augustine adds that the rebuke should be in love, not eager to wound but anxious to amend, warning that a man who passes the fault by becomes the worse of the two.

Why privately, and for what sins, are pressed separately. Augustine makes the privacy follow from the offence: if you alone know the trespass and rebuke him before all, you do not correct but betray him; faults done before all are rebuked before all, those done in private in private, by which rule the Scriptures are consistent. Jerome distinguishes the wrong done to us, which we must forgive, from that done to God, which is not ours to decide, and observes that we do the contrary, merciful where God is affronted and prosecuting where we are. Raban guards the other side: forgiveness is not commanded indiscriminately but toward him who will hearken and do penitence, so it is neither unattainable nor too far relaxed. Origen states the hardest question and refuses both answers: one man, looking to infinite mercy, says the words distinguish no sins, another that they cannot cover the great sins, a man guilty of those being not a brother but only called one; yet the first encourages the careless and the second too great severity, since we cannot decide that a man finally perishes, and he who is thrice told may hearken the fourth time. Henry gives the practical reason for privacy: to convince a man you must not expose him, which only exasperates and makes the reproof look like revenge. Great sins, he adds, amuse and silence conscience: David's heart smote him for Saul's skirt and for numbering the people, but not for Uriah till Nathan said, Thou art the man.

Telling the church is the chapter's largest modern question. Ellicott observes the word recurs here and only here after the promise to Peter; the true rendering he holds to be congregation, as every English version from Tyndale had it until the Rhemish translators brought in church, so the appeal is to the society itself and not its rulers, and a man who defies its judgment practically excommunicates himself. Barnes allows either the whole assembly or those authorized to try such cases, noting the synagogue's bench of elders. Clarke would lay the matter before the congregation of the place, or the minister and elders as its representatives. Robertson takes it for the local body, not the general, and asks whether an actual assembly is meant or the churches organized later.

Lightfoot declines the long dispute and shifts the ground, holding the business to be less the censure of the sinner than the vindication of the reprover, since the witnesses could not testify to a sin they knew nothing of but could testify that due reproof was used. The Gloss makes excommunication follow, pronounced by the Church's mouth through the priest, the whole Church working in him. Against any harshness, Augustine insists that while such a man is no longer reckoned among the brethren his salvation is not to be neglected, since we do not number the heathen among the brethren yet always seek theirs. Barnes says the same: religious intercourse ceases but not kindness or aid in affliction, owed to all men. Ellicott refuses to let the Pharisees' treatment of the heathen stand as the pattern, such men being still men and entitled to courtesy and all kindly offices.
18:
Jerome explains why the promise follows the sentence: the brother so contemned might answer, if you despise me I will despise you, so the power is conferred that the apostles may be sure man's sentence is ratified by God's. Chrysostom marks who is not addressed: it is not said to the Church's head, Bind such a man, but if you shall bind him the bonds shall be indissoluble, the thing left to discretion; and he sets the incorrigible under a twofold necessity, the casting out here and the binding in heaven, so lessening his brother's anger. Augustine adds the condition: when you hold a man as a publican you bind him on earth, but must bind with just cause, an unjust cause breaking rightful bonds; when you have corrected and agreed with him you have loosed him, conferring the boon not on yourself but on him. Henry qualifies the ratification: ministers are owned while they adhere to Christ's laws, the key not turning the wrong way. He will not have them judges and lords, the saying being not that what they decree shall be done but what they agree to ask of God; pass no sentence, he urges, you cannot in faith ask God to confirm.

What binding and loosing meant is the sharpest philological dispute. Clarke reports that Christian interpreters generally restrain the words to discipline and authority, and argues against them from the Mishna and later rabbins, where binding declares a thing unlawful and loosing lawful; the pronouns are neuter in both places, whatsoever thing and not whosoever, so the words are of things and not persons. He credits the interpretation to Lightfoot, quoting the formula by which the Jews set a man apart to teach: take thou liberty to teach what is bound and what is loose. Lightfoot himself takes the fuller sense, authority to bind and loose anything that seemed them good under the Spirit's guidance, claiming none but the apostles was ever led into all truth, they alone delivering a rule of faith to the church. Origen reads one word closely: Christ says in heaven and not, as to Peter, in the heavens, the rest not having yet attained the like perfection.

The agreement of the two is pressed as a condition. Origen says Christ does not say he will be but that he is in the midst, since as soon as they agree he is among them, and explains the failure of prayer by the want of that agreement, in doctrine and life alike: as in music, unless the voices are in time there is no pleasure to the hearer, so in the Church, unless united, God is not pleased. Chrysostom gives four reasons why agreeing men do not obtain: they ask what is not expedient, bring not their own part, pray seeking vengeance, and seek mercy for sinners who have not repented. The Gloss widens the ratification from excommunication to every petition offered by men holding together in the Church's unity.

Two moderns take the last clause as a proof of deity. Clarke sets beside it the rabbinic saying that wherever even two sit in discourse concerning the law the divine presence is among them, then presses the argument: none but God could say these words with truth, since God alone is everywhere present, and if millions of assemblies were gathered in one moment the promise puts Jesus in each; yet Jesus says the words, and therefore is God. Barnes draws the same conclusion by enumeration: at one hour two or three are assembled in every city across the world with Jesus in the midst of them all, impossible unless he be God. Chrysostom had fixed the condition: it is not said barely where they are gathered but in my name, so the man who makes Christ the chief motive of his love to his neighbour has him present.
21:
Jerome traces the question to what went before, the warning against despising the little ones and the rule for a brother who sins, which led Peter to ask and then answer himself. Lightfoot measures it against the schools, which forbade a wronged man to be difficult to pardon, that not being the manner of the seed of Israel, and praised the readiest to forgive; but he finds a snake under it, for they pardoned once, twice, thrice, and the fourth time they did not. Barnes and Clarke report the limit as three times and no fourth, so Peter more than doubled the received charity. Ellicott thinks the sacred number suggested itself as the natural limit, perhaps with a half-conscious memory of the prophet, that for three transgressions and four the punishment should not turn away. Robertson quotes Plummer, that a man who asks such a question does not know what forgiveness means. Henry is sharpest on the keeping of count: there is ill-nature in scoring up the injuries we forgive, as if we would allow ourselves revenge when the measure is full, for God keeps account, being the Judge, and we must not, lest we step into his throne.

Whether the answer is a number at all comes next. Chrysostom denies it, holding no limit is set but something endless and ever enduring; in his homily he supplies Peter's reasoning, that for the unrepentant a limit was fixed by the words about the heathen and the publican, but for him who is told his fault and repents none has been given. Wesley answers in a line: as often as there is occasion, a certain number put for an uncertain. Ellicott holds the symbolic numbers designed to lead the questioner from any numerical standard, since as there is no limit to God's forgiveness there should be none to man's, the very asking showing he had not apprehended the former. Calvin finds the objection natural to the flesh, that if we forgive so readily our lenity will induce others to offend us, and observes that Christ, far from yielding, declares expressly there ought to be no limit.

The arithmetic is nevertheless worked out differently. Robertson grants it is unclear whether the idiom means seventy-seven or four hundred and ninety, notes the same ambiguity in the Greek of Genesis, and says it matters little since unlimited forgiveness is meant either way, quoting that the unlimited revenge of primitive man has given place to the unlimited forgiveness of Christians. Jerome takes the larger figure. Augustine takes the smaller and reads it symbolically: the law is signified by ten and sin by eleven, because it passes the denary line, while seven stands for a whole since time goes round in seven days, eleven taken seven times yielding the number. Clarke sets the words beside the boast of Lamech, where the same phrase is used of vengeance, and turns the sum on the reader: let a man search ever so accurately and he will not find four hundred and ninety such offences in his whole life, an offence properly so called being given wantonly, without provocation.

What kind of forgiveness is meant is sorted last. Origen refuses the literal reckoning as silly and unworthy both of Peter's progress and the divine magnanimity of Jesus, offering instead that six denotes toil and seven repose, so pardon belongs to brethren who sin in things of this world. Augustine will not stop at any figure: if a man sin seventy-eight times forgive him, and if a hundred, however often, for if Christ found a thousand sins and forgave all, do not you withdraw your forgiveness. Raban distinguishes two pardons: one to a brother who seeks it, that he may live with us in social charity, as Joseph to his brethren, and one to a hostile foe, that we may wish him good, as David mourning Saul.
23:
Chrysostom reads the parable as a guard on the command just given, lest any think the Lord had enjoined something burdensome in requiring endless pardon. Jerome notes the Syrian custom of adding a parable, so that what a bare precept cannot hold may be held by example. Calvin says the doctrine needed confirming because it is hard to bend us to mercy and we weary quickly in bearing many faults of brethren; those who will not pardon judge very ill for themselves, subjecting themselves to a law equally stern. He rests the likeness on three contrasts: king against servant, large sum against ordinary, extraordinary kindness against extreme cruelty.

What the king is divides them. Origen takes the kingdom of heaven to be the Son himself, who as he is wisdom and righteousness and truth is also a kingdom, not of things beneath but of all above, reigning in every thought of the man no longer under sin's reign; the reckoning is his return at the consummation. Remigius takes it for the holy Church, Gill for the Gospel church state. On the servants, Barnes guesses collectors of revenue, since kings farmed out a province's taxes, so a high priest might buy those of Judea cheaply and oppress in the collecting; Clarke arrives by arithmetic, no hired servant being able to owe such a sum, so a tributary prince.

No two agree what ten thousand talents is. Barnes makes the talent three thousand shekels and the whole sixteen million dollars; Clarke calls it a myriad, the highest number in Greek notation, worth four and a half million sterling in silver or sixty-seven and a half in gold, equal to the annual revenue of the British empire; Ellicott, from the Greek translators' use for the Hebrew weight, gets two and a half million; Robertson reckons a thousand dollars the talent, and notes the imperial taxes of Judea, Idumea, and Samaria came to six hundred a year. Ellicott draws the lesson from the disagreement: the sum is named in its vague vastness. Wesley says it intimates the weight of our offences and our incapacity of satisfying God. Augustine finds the figure in the law: it is set forth in ten precepts, so ten thousand talents denote all sins doable under it, the hundred denarii keeping that number, a hundred hundreds being ten thousand and ten tens a hundred. Raban reads the debtor allegorically as the people bound to the ten commandments. Henry adds a fifth figure, one million eight hundred and seventy-five thousand pounds, and makes conscience the auditor that, unless bribed, will not write fifty for a hundred; the scripture concluding all under sin he calls a statute of bankruptcy against us all.

Barnes, Clarke, and Robertson ground the selling in the law, which let a debtor be sold with wife and children; Barnes warns against pressing that clause, thrown in to keep the story consistent and explain the servant's anxiety for delay, and Ellicott draws the framework from human laws whose details need not be pressed. Gill turns the insolvency into doctrine: a debt of sin cannot be discharged by a debt of obedience, God having a prior right to the latter, and sin against an infinite God contracts an infinite debt no creature can pay. Clarke reads the plea as fourfold: deep humiliation, fervent prayer, confidence in mercy, a purpose to devote soul and body. Ellicott will not grant so much, calling the promise an idle boast which yet aptly describes the first impulse of one roused to a sense of sin, who tries to balance the account by instalments, scoring future righteousness against past transgression and seeking to be justified by works; the compassion meets him with more than he asked, and so far he is justified by faith. Gill insists the motive lay in the king's own goodness, not in anything the man said or did.
28:
The hundred pence are a hundred denarii: Barnes prices them at fourteen dollars, Clarke and Henry at some three pounds, while Robertson lists attempts from fifty shillings to twenty pounds. Henry presses the comparison hard: dishonours done to a man like ourselves are motes and gnats, dishonours done to God talents and beams and camels, which excuses not wronging a neighbour, only our aggravating it when wronged. Ellicott alone resists the flattening. The sum is no trifle but a hundred days' wages; had a mere antithesis been wanted, some small coin would have served, whereas to the fishermen of Galilee this was a really considerable sum. So the parable grants that offences between brothers may be many and grievous in themselves, sinking into insignificance only beside sins against God.

On the violence all agree; only the idiom differs. Clarke knows no word rendering the Greek so fully as the Anglo-saxon throttle, to half choke a man by seizing his throat; Robertson makes the tense inchoative, he began to throttle him, notes that Roman law allowed the indignity, and renders the words if thou owest anything, however little, the if being a pitiless logic. Henry asks what need there was of all this, the debt being demandable without taking the debtor by the throat, and finds pride and malice more productive of severity than necessity: the carriage lordly, the spirit base. Ellicott finds the course as unwise as ungenerous: a slave cannot have his fellow-slave sold, and imprisoning him cuts off the very means of payment, so the vindictiveness is suicidal, harshness shutting an offender up as in a prison of sullen defiance. Can a man really pardoned become thus merciless? Too fatally often, he answers: not consciously a hypocrite but as yet double minded, justified and not sanctified.

Barnes stops the allegory at the fellow-servants, their report being thrown in to keep the narrative consistent, since God needs no informing of what his children do; pressing every detail abuses the parable, whose one truth is the duty of forgiveness. Ellicott notes they are called exceeding sorry rather than angry, sorrow being the disciple's mood before the scandals of the Christian society, wrath belonging to the Judge. Henry holds that what gives occasion for sorrow should give occasion for prayer; Robertson, that there is a limit to what people will put up with. Gill puts the reproof simply: it is but reasonable that such as have received mercy should show mercy.

The tormentors divide them. Barnes keeps them jailers, since torments were inflicted on criminals and not debtors, and takes the punishment to be imprisonment only. Clarke will have the tortures themselves, such as the Asiatics used on a suspected fraud, then turns them inward to a guilty conscience and a fearful looking for of fiery indignation. Ellicott thinks the words deliberately vague, daring not make the tormentors avenging angels or demons, but whatever agencies God employs in retribution: the stings of remorse, the scorn of men, what lies behind the veil. Calvin and Robertson both refuse the Roman reading, Calvin calling it ridiculous to light the fire of purgatory from the word, eternal and not temporal death being meant, Robertson agreeing it is punitive and not purgatorial. Whether the pardon was revoked divides them most sharply. Wesley says plainly the pardon was retracted and the whole debt required, and asks whether we may still say a pardon once given can never be retracted. Ellicott agrees: the debt may come back, faith that does not work by love ceases to justify, and the discharge is traced as in sympathetic ink, appearing and disappearing with the debtor's faith and love. Henry wrote of the pardon revoked and the acquittance cancelled, but at the last will not have God reverse his pardons, only deny them to the unqualified, who had seemed humbled and thought themselves pardoned already.
